summary:
Île-de-France stands under the French national framework: identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law, care access and marriage are set nationally and apply uniformly across the region, and no separate regional regime governs transgender visitors. What is specific to the region is where recorded anti-LGBT+ offending falls and how the Paris agglomeration's LGBT venues and events are policed.

The Interior Ministry's statistics service (SSMSI), in Infraction rapide n°53 of May 2025, records 4,800 anti-LGBT+ offences across France in 2024, up 5% on 2023, with crimes and délits rising 14% per year since 2016. Only about 4% of victims file complaints, so the recorded figure understates incidence. Acts concentrate in urban units of over 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris, whose rate is 22 per 100,000 against a national rate of 7; the note attributes part of Paris's elevated rate to non-resident victims and commuters. Recorded victims are more than 70% men, so the statistics do not isolate trans victims.

Large LGBT events in the Paris agglomeration now carry a documented far-right counter-presence and a heavy security response. The Paris Pride march (Marche des Fiertés) of 28 June 2025 was classed a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry, and CRS police reinforcements were deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march; police were framed as separating the opposing groups, with extremists described as the enemy.

Paris holds France's densest LGBTQ infrastructure, including France's only officially organised gaybourhoods and the annual Paris Pride parade. As of 2004 the city had 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops. The city also carries a targeted-violence history: Bertrand Delanoë, who became France's first openly gay mayor of Paris in 2002, was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals. This is the most recent documented anti-LGBT political assault in this record; no later instance is documented here.
tangentialFactors:
Paris's high recorded anti-LGBT+ offence rate (22 per 100,000 in 2024 against a national 7) partly reflects non-resident victims and commuters passing through the capital, so the figure measures exposure in the agglomeration rather than risk to residents alone. A visitor moving through central Paris is counted in the same denominator as the resident population.

Paris Pride and comparable agglomeration events are now managed as sensitive events with riot-police reinforcement and physical separation of counter-demonstrators, which changes the security atmosphere around LGBT gatherings without changing their legal status.
localsOnly:
For residents, the SSMSI figures are the operative measure of recorded offending: 4,800 anti-LGBT+ offences nationally in 2024, with Paris the leading urban unit, and a complaint rate of about 4% meaning most incidents never enter the statistics. Recorded victims are more than 70% men, so services built on these figures may under-serve trans and female victims.

Local LGBT infrastructure in Paris is dense by national standards, with organised gaybourhoods and an annual Pride march, but the 2002 stabbing of Mayor Bertrand Delanoë and the 2025 counter-presence at Pride indicate that visibility attracts targeted hostility.
outOfScopeNotes:
The SSMSI note's Paris rate is not broken down by victim gender identity, so no trans-specific offending rate for Île-de-France is available in this inventory; the >70% male victim share is LGBT-wide, not trans-specific.

The 140-venue figure for Paris dates from 2004 and is not refreshed in this inventory; current venue counts are unresolved here.

The Delanoë stabbing is the most recent documented anti-LGBT political assault in this record, from 2002; no later instance is documented, and the absence of later cases here does not establish their absence in fact.
